Mortality: a binomial response and a neural-network process

Source: vignettes/E-Mortality.Rmd
E-Mortality.Rmd

Mortality is the hardest of FINN’s six responses to calibrate, and the one where the choice of likelihood matters most. This vignette takes it on its own terms: what the observation actually is, which likelihood belongs to it, how to swap the process for a neural network, and (the part that is easy to get wrong) how to score the result.

It follows the same 200-fit / 200-holdout FIA sample as Fitting FINN to forest inventory data, and like that page it is precompiled by vignettes/build.R: the models below are really trained.

library(FINN)
library(torch)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

EPOCHS <- 500L

Mortality is a proportion, not a rate

makeObsData() returns mortality as a pair of counts rather than a bare rate:

  • n_at_risk: trees alive at the start of an inventory interval,
  • n_died: how many of those were dead at the end,

with the yearly rate mort = 1 - (1 - n_died / n_at_risk)^(1 / period_length) derived from them: FINN simulates yearly steps, and an inventory interval of period_length years is that many simulated years, whose yearly mortalities fit() compounds into the same per-year rate before it meets the observation. The counts are exactly the cbind(died, survived) response of a binomial GLM, and it is deliberate. A bare proportion throws away the sample size: it cannot tell a site where 1 of 1 trees died from one where 60 of 60 did, even though the second carries sixty times the information.

The pair is a closed cohort; both columns are pinned to the tree’s state at the start of the interval. That matters more than it sounds. FIA re-identifies a tree’s species between visits, so a rate built by dividing “deaths this year” by “survivors last year” can book a death against the species a tree ended as while the denominator counted the species it started as, and report more deaths than there were trees. Pinning both columns to the interval start makes n_died <= n_at_risk true by construction. (Trees that recruit during the interval are in neither column; see ?makeObsData for the open-cohort alternative.)

# The tables ship with FINN as datasets (?fia_obs_dt), already in FINN's input
# format, so there is nothing to read or prepare.

# --- training sites --------------------------------------------------------
obs_dt     <- fia_obs_dt        # observations, wide (one column per variable)
env_dt     <- fia_env_dt        # RAW, untransformed climate
init_trees <- fia_init_trees
species_dt <- fia_species_dt

# --- holdout sites: never seen during fitting ------------------------------
obs_test   <- fia_obs_test
env_test   <- fia_env_test
init_test  <- fia_init_test

obs_dt[, .(siteID, year, period_length, species_name, n_at_risk, n_died, mort)][n_at_risk > 0][1:6]
#>    siteID  year period_length          species_name n_at_risk n_died      mort
#>     <int> <int>         <int>                <char>     <int>  <int>     <num>
#> 1:      1    10            10 Pseudotsuga menziesii         2      0 0.0000000
#> 2:      1    10            10         Abies grandis         6      0 0.0000000
#> 3:      1    10            10                 other         3      1 0.0397355
#> 4:      1    20            10 Pseudotsuga menziesii         2      0 0.0000000
#> 5:      1    20            10         Abies grandis        10      0 0.0000000
#> 6:      1    20            10                 other         2      0 0.0000000

How much mortality signal is actually in this sample? Less than the number of rows suggests:

cat(sprintf("observations with a cohort at risk : %d\n", obs_dt[n_at_risk > 0, .N]))
#> observations with a cohort at risk : 1003
cat(sprintf("of which mort is exactly zero      : %d (%.0f%%)\n",
            obs_dt[n_at_risk > 0 & n_died == 0, .N],
            100 * obs_dt[n_at_risk > 0, mean(n_died == 0)]))
#> of which mort is exactly zero      : 688 (69%)
cat(sprintf("trees at risk (train)              : %d\n", obs_dt[, sum(n_at_risk)]))
#> trees at risk (train)              : 9907
cat(sprintf("deaths (train)                     : %d\n", obs_dt[, sum(n_died)]))
#> deaths (train)                     : 656
cat(sprintf("pooled mortality                   : %.3f over the ten-year interval, %.4f per year\n",
            obs_dt[, sum(n_died) / sum(n_at_risk)],
            obs_dt[, 1 - (1 - sum(n_died) / sum(n_at_risk))^(1 / 10)]))
#> pooled mortality                   : 0.066 over the ten-year interval, 0.0068 per year

A few hundred deaths, and roughly two-thirds of the observations at exactly zero. No likelihood can manufacture information that is not there, but the wrong one can waste what is.

Why binomial and not mse

FINN scores mortality with loss_family = c(..., mortality = "binomial", ...) by default. Squared error assumes an unbounded response with constant variance; mortality is neither. A proportion lives on 0,10, 1 and its variance shrinks as the rate approaches either end, so on a response that is ~69% zeros, MSE puts almost no gradient where the data actually are.

The binomial term is weighted by n_at_risk, which is what turns a Bernoulli term into a binomial one. It is the same thing R does with glm(prop ~ ., family = binomial, weights = n).

Two models: mechanistic mortality, and mortality as a network 

Nsp          <- uniqueN(obs_dt$species)
init_cohorts      <- makeInitCohorts(init_trees, Nspecies = Nsp)
init_cohorts_test <- makeInitCohorts(init_test,  Nspecies = Nsp)
# shared colours for the two model variants, reused below
model_cols <- c("Process (mechanistic)" = "#1b9e77", "Hybrid (mortality = NN)" = "#7570b3")

The mechanistic baseline, with all four processes in their functional form:

FINN.seed(42)
m <- finn(
  N_species            = Nsp,
  recruits_dbh         = 12.9,   # DBH (cm) assigned to a new recruit; ~ FIA's 12.7 cm (5 in) minimum
  competition_process  = createProcess(~0, FINN::competition,  optimizeSpecies = TRUE),
  growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::growth,       optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),
  regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::regeneration_capped, optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),
  mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::mortality,    optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE)
)
fit(m,
  env = env_dt, data = obs_dt, init_cohort = init_cohorts, device = "cpu",
  epochs = EPOCHS, batchsize = 40L, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06,
  lr = 0.01, env_autoscale = TRUE, plot_progress = FALSE
)

Now the same model with mortality replaced by a neural network, every other process, and the entire fit() call, unchanged. createHybrid() is the only difference:

FINN.seed(42)
m_mort <- finn(
  N_species            = Nsp,
  recruits_dbh         = 12.9,
  competition_process  = createProcess(~0, FINN::competition,  optimizeSpecies = TRUE),
  growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::growth,       optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),
  regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::regeneration_capped, optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),
  mortality_process    = createHybrid(~ temp + prec, hidden = c(20L, 20L), transformer = FALSE)
)
fit(m_mort,
  env = env_dt, data = obs_dt, init_cohort = init_cohorts, device = "cpu",
  epochs = EPOCHS, batchsize = 40L, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06,
  lr = 0.01, env_autoscale = TRUE, plot_progress = FALSE
)

Scoring mortality: why not Spearman

The model simulates yearly steps, so its mortality is compared with an observation as fit() compares it: the simulated yearly mortalities of the period_length years before the census compounded into one rate per year, 1 - exp(mean(log1p(-m))), the functional behind the observed 1 - (1 - n_died / n_at_risk)^(1 / period_length).

evaluate() does this pairing. It simulates the model on the sites it was fitted to and, with holdout, on sites it has not seen, aggregates every response the way fit() scores it, and keeps the paired table ($matched) and the skill measures ($skill) of each set. The result is also stored on the model, where summary() reads it.

holdout <- list(data = obs_test, env = env_test, init_cohort = init_cohorts_test)
m$eval(); m_mort$eval()
FINN.seed(1)
ev      <- evaluate(m,      holdout = holdout)
ev_mort <- evaluate(m_mort, holdout = holdout)

# the paired mortality cells of both models on both sets
mort_of <- function(ev, label)
  rbind(ev$train$matched[variable == "mort"][, `:=`(model = label, split = "train")],
        ev$holdout$matched[variable == "mort"][, `:=`(model = label, split = "holdout")])
mort_pred <- rbind(mort_of(ev,      "Process (mechanistic)"),
                   mort_of(ev_mort, "Hybrid (mortality = NN)"))
mort_pred[1:3, .(siteID, year, species_name, period_length, n_at_risk, n_died, obs, pred, p_interval)]
#>    siteID  year          species_name period_length n_at_risk n_died       obs
#>     <int> <int>                <char>         <num>     <int>  <int>     <num>
#> 1:      1    10 Pseudotsuga menziesii            10         2      0 0.0000000
#> 2:      1    10         Abies grandis            10         6      0 0.0000000
#> 3:      1    10                 other            10         3      1 0.0397355
#>            pred p_interval
#>           <num>      <num>
#> 1: 0.0003227343 0.00322266
#> 2: 0.0022701982 0.02247146
#> 3: 0.0050098909 0.04898441

Each row is one site, census and species: the observed yearly rate obs, the simulated yearly rate pred compounded over the interval, and p_interval, the probability that a tree dies over the whole interval, 1 - (1 - pred)^period_length.

Rank correlation is the natural first reach, and it is a trap here. Two-thirds of the observed proportions are exactly zero, so Spearman spends most of its power ranking ties against each other; a value near zero cannot distinguish “the model learned nothing” from “the metric cannot see what it learned”.

mort_pred[, .(spearman = round(cor(obs, pred, method = "spearman"), 2), n = .N),
          by = .(model, split)][order(split, model)]
#>                      model   split spearman     n
#>                     <char>  <char>    <num> <int>
#> 1: Hybrid (mortality = NN) holdout     0.07   994
#> 2:   Process (mechanistic) holdout     0.03   994
#> 3: Hybrid (mortality = NN)   train     0.21  1003
#> 4:   Process (mechanistic)   train     0.20  1003

AUC asks the question the binomial actually poses: does the model give a higher death probability to a tree that died than to one that survived? Each observation stands for n_at_risk Bernoulli trials of which n_died are deaths, all sharing that observation’s predicted probability of death over the interval, so rather than expand the trials we weight them, with tied predictions taking half credit (the standard Mann-Whitney treatment). Written out:

auc_binom <- function(p, pos, neg) {
  g <- data.table(p = p, pos = pos, neg = neg)[
    , .(pos = sum(pos), neg = sum(neg)), by = p][order(p)]
  neg_below <- cumsum(g$neg) - g$neg              # negatives strictly below each p
  den <- sum(g$pos) * sum(g$neg)
  if (den == 0) return(NA_real_)
  sum(g$pos * (neg_below + 0.5 * g$neg)) / den    # 0.5 credit for ties
}

auc_tab <- mort_pred[n_at_risk > 0,
  .(AUC     = round(auc_binom(p_interval, n_died, n_at_risk - n_died), 3),
    deaths  = sum(n_died),
    at_risk = sum(n_at_risk)), by = .(model, split)]
auc_tab[order(split, -AUC)]
#>                      model   split   AUC deaths at_risk
#>                     <char>  <char> <num>  <int>   <int>
#> 1: Hybrid (mortality = NN) holdout 0.537    727   10013
#> 2:   Process (mechanistic) holdout 0.524    727   10013
#> 3: Hybrid (mortality = NN)   train 0.643    656    9907
#> 4:   Process (mechanistic)   train 0.639    656    9907

0.5 is coin-flipping, 1.0 is perfect ranking. evaluate() computes the same AUC in its skill table, next to the ratio of the predicted to the observed deaths (the expected deaths n_at_risk * p_interval summed over the cells):

skill_of <- function(ev, label)
  rbind(ev$train$skill[variable == "mort", .(model = label, split = "train", AUC = round(auc, 3),
                                             deaths_ratio = round(deaths_ratio, 2))],
        ev$holdout$skill[variable == "mort", .(model = label, split = "holdout", AUC = round(auc, 3),
                                               deaths_ratio = round(deaths_ratio, 2))])
rbind(skill_of(ev, "Process (mechanistic)"), skill_of(ev_mort, "Hybrid (mortality = NN)"))
#>                      model   split   AUC deaths_ratio
#>                     <char>  <char> <num>        <num>
#> 1:   Process (mechanistic)   train 0.639         1.30
#> 2:   Process (mechanistic) holdout 0.524         1.25
#> 3: Hybrid (mortality = NN)   train 0.643         0.43
#> 4: Hybrid (mortality = NN) holdout 0.537         0.45

plot() of the evaluation draws the ROC curve behind it, here of the mechanistic model on the holdout (response keeps the mortality panel only; without it the page also shows the other responses):

plot(ev, response = "mort")

and on its training sites:

plot(ev, response = "mort", set = "train")

summary() prints the skill tables of both sets with the AUC, followed by the convergence of the fit and the environmental effects. The environmental effects take long on all 200 training sites, so env and init_cohort give them a subset of 30 sites:

xai_sites <- sort(unique(env_dt$siteID))[1:30]
env_xai   <- env_dt[siteID %in% xai_sites]
init_xai  <- makeInitCohorts(init_trees[siteID %in% xai_sites], Nspecies = Nsp)
summary(m, env = env_xai, init_cohort = init_xai)

Read the two splits together, because the gap between them is the result. On the training sites the models rank deaths above survivors better than chance (AUC 0.64 and 0.64), so there is a learnable mortality signal, and the models find it. On the held-out sites that skill falls to 0.52 and 0.54, close to 0.5. The model is not failing to fit mortality; it is fitting it and not generalising.

That is what a few hundred deaths buys. With ~69% of observations at exactly zero and mortality concentrated in whichever species happened to die on whichever plot, there is enough signal to memorise and not enough to transfer. The network variant and the mechanistic process rank alike on the holdout, both close to coin-flipping and far below their training skill, so neither transfers.

So mortality here is honestly reported as not identified out-of-sample. The binomial likelihood is the right loss for a proportion and the closed cohort is the right response, but neither manufactures information the two inventories do not contain. Treat differences between the two models as noise; the signal worth reading is train-vs-holdout, not model-vs-model.

Scoring each tree instead of each cell

Everything above scores mortality per cell: the model’s mean death probability over the cohorts of a site, census and species against the pooled proportion. That mean has a compositional confound. Mortality falls several-fold from the smallest to the largest trees, so the cell mean moves when the simulated size distribution moves, whether or not the hazard function is right, and a mortality parameter can end up correcting a growth or recruitment error. With a tree list in hand, fit() can instead score the fate of every observed tree: loss_aggregation = c(mortality = "tree") runs the mortality kernel on each tree at its measured diameter, with light from the observed stand, and compares the death probability over the interval with the tree’s 0/1 fate. It measures the mortality function alone, teacher-forced onto the observed stands, and combines with the simulated dbh, ba, trees and regeneration terms (see ?fit, section Scoring individual trees, for the other per-tree route and when each applies).

Prefer it when the trees are available and mortality is the response of interest: it uses every tree as a trial rather than a few hundred cells, it is unaffected by how well the stand is simulated, and predictTrees() evaluates the same code path, so a validation cannot drift from the objective it checks. Its cost is that the scored mortality is no longer a property of the simulated trajectory.

The bundled sample carries the tree fates as fia_tree_dt and fia_tree_test, and the Fitting FINN to forest inventory data vignette fits the 200 sites with this route and reports the holdout AUC and the mortality by size class. Here the mechanism is shown on a tree list built from raw data, the eight Oregon FIA plots of the Preparing your data for FINN vignette, four patches each, three inventories. makeObsData() already derives each tree’s start-of-interval state, so tree_data is a selection of its columns. The year of a row is the census that closes the interval, dbh the diameter at its start, died the fate over it; trees that recruited during the interval were not at risk and stay out.

tree_raw <- fread(system.file("extdata", "example_tree_dt.csv", package = "FINN"))
prep <- makeObsData(tree_raw[complete == TRUE], plotsize = 0.06, aggregate_by_site = FALSE,
                    fix_period_length = 10, NspeciesQuantile = 0.98)
inputs <- resolveSiteIDs(tree_dt = prep$tree_dt, obs_dt = prep$obs_dt,
                         env_dt = fread(system.file("extdata", "example_env_dt.csv", package = "FINN")))
tree_data <- inputs$tree_dt[year > 0 & living_before == TRUE,
  .(siteID, year, patchID, species, dbh = dbh_before, growth,
    died = as.numeric(status == "dead"), period_length)]
tree_data[, .(trees = .N, died = sum(died)), by = .(year, period_length)]
#>     year period_length trees  died
#>    <int>         <int> <int> <num>
#> 1:    10            10   130     9
#> 2:    20            10   127    12

Two details of the set-up. growth is the tree’s yearly growth rate that makeObsData() computed, and period_length the ten years of its interval: the tree route runs the mortality kernel over every simulated year of the interval and compares the compounded death probability 1 - prod(1 - m) with the tree’s fate. The per-tree term is accumulated over each site’s observation window, which fit() reads from the period_length column of data, which resolveSiteIDs() returns. And the model is the mechanistic one from above, with the mortality term alone switched to the tree route:

obs_8 <- inputs$obs_dt
Nsp_8 <- nrow(inputs$species_dt)

FINN.seed(42)
m_tree <- finn(
  N_species            = Nsp_8, recruits_dbh = 12.9,
  competition_process  = createProcess(~0, FINN::competition,  optimizeSpecies = TRUE),
  growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::growth,       optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),
  regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::regeneration_capped, optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),
  mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::mortality,    optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE)
)
fit(m_tree,
  env = inputs$env_dt, data = obs_8, init_cohort = inputs$initCohorts, device = "cpu",
  epochs = EPOCHS, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06, lr = 0.01, plot_progress = FALSE,
  loss_aggregation = c(mortality = "tree"),   # growth and the state terms stay per cell
  tree_data        = tree_data
)

predictTrees() returns one row per row of tree_data, in the same order, so the predictions are bound on rather than joined. Each tree is one Bernoulli trial, so the AUC needs no weighting here; it is the same auc_binom() with one trial per row:

m_tree$eval()
tree_pred <- cbind(tree_data,
                   predictTrees(m_tree, tree_data = tree_data, env = inputs$env_dt)[, .(mort_pred)])
tree_pred[, .(trees = .N, deaths = sum(died),
              AUC = round(auc_binom(mort_pred, died, 1 - died), 3)), by = year]
#>     year trees deaths   AUC
#>    <int> <int>  <num> <num>
#> 1:    10   130      9 0.941
#> 2:    20   127     12 0.936

Eight plots and two dozen deaths are a demonstration of the mechanism, not a mortality model, and the trees scored are the trees fitted; the 200-site fit with its holdout is in the Fitting FINN to forest inventory data vignette. What the route buys shows in a drought or disturbance study, where the question is how the hazard of a tree of a given size and species responds to the environment, and the cell mean would let the simulated size distribution answer instead.

What the network learned: ALE

ALE() returns one table per process, so the same tool reads a mechanistic mortality function and a neural network standing in its place. The effect is on the yearly mortality probability.

We read the effects over the same 30 training sites as summary() above (without env and init_cohort, ALE() uses all training sites the model keeps from fit()). plot() draws the environmental drivers, one line per species, here for the network:

ale_proc <- ALE(m,      env = env_xai, init_cohort = init_xai, plot = FALSE)
ale_hyb  <- ALE(m_mort, env = env_xai, init_cohort = init_xai, plot = FALSE)
plot(ale_hyb, process = "mortality")

To compare the two models on the same axes, we put both tables together, on the natural scale of the climate drivers:


to_natural <- function(a, model) {
  sc <- as.data.table(model$env_scaling)[, .(var = variable, center, scale)]
  merge(data.table(a), sc, by = "var", all.x = TRUE)[!is.na(center), x := x * scale + center]
}
mortality <- rbind(
  to_natural(ale_proc$mortality, m)[,      model := "Process (mechanistic)"],
  to_natural(ale_hyb$mortality,  m_mort)[, model := "Hybrid (mortality = NN)"])
mortality <- merge(mortality, species_dt, by = "species")
d <- mortality[var %in% c("dbh", "light", "temp") & species %in% c(1, 2, 4, 5)]
d[, var := factor(var, levels = c("dbh", "light", "temp"))]
ggplot(d, aes(x, ale, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_grid(species_name ~ var, scales = "free",
             labeller = labeller(
               var = as_labeller(c(dbh = "diameter~(cm)", light = "light~availability",
                                   temp = "temperature~(degree*C)"), label_parsed),
               species_name = label_value)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "accumulated local effect on mortality", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0))

Each curve spans only the range its own model actually simulates (ALE never extrapolates) so where the two cover different ranges they are simply placing a species in different conditions.

Read these as a demonstration of the mechanism: a process can be replaced by a network and still be interrogated with the same tool. They are not a settled mortality response. With a few hundred deaths the network is free to flatten wherever the data do not constrain it, and a flat ALE here is as likely to mean “no signal” as “no effect”.
